source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Forever — is composed of Nows — / ’Tis not a different time, / Except for infiniteness / And latitude of home.
trail: First published posthumously in Further Poems of Emily Dickinson (1929) ↗, edited by Martha Dickinson Bianchi and Alfred Leete Hampson.
The manuscript, written in ink around 1863 as part of Dickinson’s handbound Fascicle 32, is catalogued as Franklin #690 and Johnson #624, per The Prowling Bee’s line-by-line reading ↗.
The full text is also collected by the Academy of American Poets ↗, which notes the poem is in the public domain.
source.excerptNote: Only the opening quatrain is shown; the poem continues for three more stanzas.
source.rightsNote: First published in 1929 in Further Poems of Emily Dickinson, placing this text in the U.S. public domain.

author.name: Emily Dickinson
author.heading: About Emily Dickinson
author.bio: Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems in Amherst, Massachusetts, publishing only a handful during her lifetime; almost all the rest — including this one — were discovered and published after her death in 1886. Her dash-punctuated, compressed style returns again and again to time, mortality, and the texture of consciousness.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Dickinson lived and wrote almost entirely in private, publishing fewer than a dozen poems in her lifetime. Nearly 1,800 more, hand-copied into small bound booklets known as fascicles, were found in her bedroom by her sister Lavinia after Dickinson died in 1886, and were gradually brought into print over the following decades.

This poem — four short stanzas meditating on how “forever” is nothing more than an accumulation of present moments — is one of those posthumous discoveries. It first reached readers in 1929, more than sixty years after Dickinson wrote it.
